Performance
per-form'ans
n. (the doing or carrying out of a thing; the completion of what was promised or begun)
From perform, Old French parfournir, to furnish or accomplish completely, from par- (thoroughly) and fournir, to furnish. The old sense is carrying through to completion, not a display before an audience.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences concern promises being carried through. Elisabeth says to Mary, “blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord” (Luk 1:45). The beatitude is pronounced on faith, and the ground of it is that God finishes what He announces — Mary is blessed not because she achieved anything but because she believed a promise that would certainly be performed. Paul uses the word of a very ordinary matter, the Corinthian collection for the poor saints: “Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have” (2Co 8:11). Willing is not the same as doing; a readiness that never becomes a gift is unfinished, and Paul asks for the completion. Put together, the two texts hold the whole Reformed doctrine of the Christian life: God performs His promises infallibly — “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6) — and believers are therefore commanded to perform their duties really. Abraham is the pattern of the first: “being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform” (Rom 4:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines performance as the act of performing; execution or completion of any thing; the carrying into effect a promise, purpose, or covenant.

expand to see more

PERFORM'ANCE, n.

1. Execution or completion of any thing; a doing; as the performance of work or of an undertaking.

2. The fulfilment of a promise or covenant; as the performance of a vow.

3. Action; deed; thing done; as a virtuous performance.

4. Composition; work written. The old sense is to carry through to completion, from par, thoroughly, and fournir, to furnish.

Key Scripture

Luke 1:45 — "And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord."

2 Corinthians 8:11 — "Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have."

Philippians 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

Romans 4:21 — "And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform."

Modern Corruption

The word has slid from completing a promise to putting on a show, and the church has caught the disease in both directions.

expand to see more

English moved performance from the covenant to the stage, and the church followed. A worship service is now assessed the way a concert is: the music performed, the sermon delivered, the room responding. Luke 1:45 uses the word for something no audience watches — a promise being carried through over nine months in an unmarried girl in Nazareth. The regulative principle exists in part to keep this distinction: what is done in the assembly is done because God commanded it, which means no one on the platform is performing and no one in the pews is an audience.

The opposite corruption is a lazy reading of Philippians 1:6. Because God performs the good work, it is said, the believer's own performing does not much matter — and effort is treated as a hint of legalism. 2 Corinthians 8:11 is unembarrassed: Paul tells a willing church to go and actually do it. The Reformed order is God works, therefore you work (Php 2:12-13), never God works, therefore you need not. A readiness to will that never yields a performance is not humility about grace; it is an unfinished obedience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek teleiosis (G5050), a completing, fulfilment; epiteleo (G2005), to finish, accomplish; Old French parfournir, to furnish completely.

expand to see more

Greek teleiosis (G5050) — completion, fulfilment; Luke 1:45, there shall be a finishing of what was told her.

Greek epitelesate (G2005) — complete it, bring it to its end; 2 Corinthians 8:11, the command to the willing.

Greek epitelesei (G2005) — He will complete it; Philippians 1:6, the same verb with God as subject.

Greek dunatos…poiesai (G1415) — able also to do; Romans 4:21, Abraham's persuasion about God's power to perform.

Old French parfournir — to furnish thoroughly; Webster's root, with completion and not display in view.

Usage

"“There shall be a performance of those things” — the beatitude rests on God finishing, not on Mary achieving."

"“A readiness to will, so there may be a performance” — willing is not yet doing."

"“Will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” — the same verb, with God as the subject."
